A job currently being worked can never be removed, and a dead job only when the call names that state, so no record of a failure disappears without a line of source saying so. Both members take the deny-by-default `queue.purge` capability; pushing, checking, cancelling and counting still take none.

entries.headline: `nvs serve` is one process for requests, schedules and jobs
entries.body: The served process runs the queue workers itself, started alongside the schedule ticker before it begins accepting connections, so `[queue] workers` in the configuration means what it says in production and no second process has to be deployed. Shutting down drains all three: in- flight requests finish, the ticker stops, and a worker stops when its current job is done. The worker count is per instance, not per core. A CLI run is unchanged.

entries.headline: A request body is read either into a buffer or as a stream, never both
entries.body: `body`, `post`, `json` and `jsonAs` buffer the request body under the configured size limit and answer from that buffer, so any of them may follow any other in any order. `bodyStream` and `files` hand the bytes to the program as they arrive and keep nothing, so each of those may only be the first thing to read the body. Reading `post()` after walking `files()` still works: the walk buffers the ordinary fields it passes, and `post()` reads that buffer like any other buffering reader.

entries.headline: A route capture typed at your own class converts in the handler, or is a 400
entries.body: The router narrows a path segment on the types it reads natively: `int`, `uint`, `decimal`, `Core\Uuid` and a few more. A segment one of those refuses is not a match, and the walk continues toward a 404. A capture declared at any other class that parses from text matches on shape only; the class's own `parse` runs where the handler reads the value, so no user code runs on URLs that matched nothing. A segment the class then refuses throws over a route that did match, which is a 400, like a bad query value.

entries.headline: The server accepts on one worker per core, and the program is compiled once
entries.body: `nvs serve` binds every listener first, then starts one worker per core, each with its own scheduler and its own accept loop over every listener. No single core hands connections out to the others, so there is no accepting core to become the bottleneck. `[server] workers` sets the count and defaults to the machine's parallelism; there is no automatic spelling. The compiled program stays one copy shared read-only by every core, so it is compiled once per source change, not once per core.

entries.headline: One socket class over three transports; the grant follows the direction
entries.body: `Core\Net` replaces PHP's three overlapping socket APIs with one class and five ways in. The capability an opening needs depends on what the program is doing, not on the transport: connecting out is `net.connect` and carries the outbound address policy, listening is `net.listen` and names endpoints, and a socket path at either end is `net.local`. UDP is datagrams and nothing more. Every socket is closed with the request that opened it. PHP's `stream_socket_pair` has no counterpart.

entries.headline: Encoding a self-containing value fails at the first repeat, naming the path
entries.body: `Core\Json::encode` and its peers remember which objects they are currently inside, and the first object met a second time on the way down ends the encoding with an error naming the property chain that closed the loop, such as `user.team.owner`. A value that merely appears twice, in two places, is written twice. The encoder never invents a marker in the document to stand for the repeat, because the document is somebody else's contract. A separate depth limit still exists, but it is no longer how a cycle is detected.

entries.headline: A log record names the line that produced it, and the file log counts repeats
entries.body: Every log record carries the file and line it was written from, and an exception's location is filled in at construction rather than left blank. When the same record repeats in a short window, the file log target merges the run into one line with a count, because a disk is what a flood would hurt. The debug stream does not merge: its store groups at read time, so every occurrence is kept. A per-line rate limit was considered and not taken.

entries.headline: XML is a whole tree or a one-window stream, and a DOCTYPE is refused outright
entries.body: `Core\Xml` offers a tree that loads the whole document and answers walks in any order, and a reader and writer that hold one element at a time. No operation is available through both, so a program picks the shape for how much of the document it needs at once and pays for that alone. There is no code that resolves an entity, so external entities are not a setting that could be left on, and a `<!DOCTYPE>` is refused whole, which ends the billion-laughs family before it starts. Nesting depth is the one numeric bound.

entries.headline: A response body can be written over time, one chunk in flight at a time
entries.body: A response is either a whole body with an exact length, as before, or a stream the handler writes to while the connection sends it. Only the stream is chunked. The writer hands over one chunk and waits until the connection has taken it before it may write the next, so a slow client cannot make the server buffer an unbounded body. The stream ends with its request; a stream that outlives the request is a separate door and is not this one.

entries.headline: An idle queue costs almost nothing
entries.body: A queue worker with no job used to check the database a hundred times per second. It now checks once per second. A job that the same process adds still starts at once, because `Core\Queue::push` wakes the workers when the job is saved. Inside a transaction, the workers are woken when the transaction commits. A job that another process adds, a job with a `runAt` time and a job that runs again after an error can start up to one second late.

groups.title: Tools, editors and shipping
groups.blurb: Everything around the language: the command-line tool, the editor experience, formatting, packaging, deployment, and what the tools may and may not do for you.

entries.headline: One language server, with thin VS Code and PhpStorm clients around it
entries.body: Completion, hover, diagnostics, rename, go-to-definition and formatting are each implemented once, in the language server and formatter that ship with the toolchain. An editor client only starts them, forwards its editor's events and shows what comes back; it decides nothing about the language. VS Code is the reference client. The PhpStorm plugin bridges to the same server rather than rebuilding the smarts in JetBrains' own framework, so PhpStorm's native formatter settings and debugger window do not apply to Novis files; a full native plugin is a later decision if usage earns it.

entries.headline: Coverage, tracing and profiling are built in and can start mid-request
entries.body: Code coverage, call tracing and a per-call profiler ship in the runtime, switched on with one setting or one `Core\Debug` call, and exported as Clover, lcov and Callgrind so the tools PHP developers already use read the output unchanged. Every compiled program carries a tiny check at each statement and each call, so turning a probe on for a running request is just flipping a flag — which lets a test harness start coverage around one test inside a long-lived process. In production the setting is a ceiling a request can never widen.

entries.headline: `nvs fmt` has one style, no configuration, and never runs unless asked
entries.body: `nvs fmt` rewrites a file into one layout. The style is PER wherever Novis matches PHP, plus a fixed layout for each construct PER never saw. It never reflows: whether a call or array spans one line or many is your choice, and only the indentation, spacing and braces around it are normalized; there is no line-length rule. There is no config file and no flag that changes output. No compiler command runs it; an unformatted file is not even a warning. `nvs fmt --check` reports what would change without touching disk.

entries.headline: VS Code is the reference editor, and the parser is built for a half-typed file
entries.body: A language server gives diagnostics, hover, go-to-definition and completion, and the VS Code extension is the client it is built against, available from the point the command-line language becomes usable. Deeper features each wait on the part of the language they depend on. Underneath, the parser never gives up on a broken file: an unclosed brace or a half-typed `$user->` still produces a tree with the invented parts marked, so completion keeps working around the error. The price is that every analysis reparses the whole document.

entries.headline: A trace shows garbage-collection pauses and sandbox spawns on one timeline
entries.body: When tracing is on, every recorded event says what kind it is: a call, a garbage-collection pause, the start or join of a spawned sandbox, or a database statement. The run exports in the format speedscope reads, so all four kinds scroll past on one timeline in an existing viewer. A stop-the-world collection shows up as its own pause instead of being charged to whatever function was running. The bookkeeping lives in routines that are already rare and slow, and costs nothing when tracing is off.

entries.headline: A command-line program can ship as one executable with its source appended
entries.body: `nvs build --compile entry.nvs -o app` produces a single file: the Novis runtime with the program's source tree appended after it and a small footer. At startup the runtime checks its own file for that footer and, if present, resolves `require` from the embedded tree instead of the disk. The executable never rewrites itself; to update the program, the author runs the same build again. This is for command-line programs only. It ships source rather than machine code, trading some startup time for one file that runs on any supported machine.

entries.headline: Server configuration is one TOML file, nvs.toml
entries.body: The server reads its configuration from a TOML file named nvs.toml, at boot and again on reload. TOML has a specification and real types, so a setting that is a boolean, a list or a repeated record is written as one rather than as a string somebody has to parse. A key that appears twice is an error, and so is a key the server does not know, which catches a typo where INI would silently ignore it. The file is not a project manifest. ini_set and ini_get become Core\Config::set and Core\Config::get.

entries.headline: Third-party licence notices are generated, committed and built into the binary
entries.body: Novis is MIT-licensed and links around eighty permissive components, every one of which asks that its notice travel with the binary. The notice file is generated from the resolved dependency graph, never written by hand, committed to the repository, and compiled into the nvs executable, so a copy handed to someone without the source still carries it. Continuous integration regenerates the file and fails the build if it differs, so a dependency added without its notice never ships. nvs info prints the build and component summary; nvs info --licenses prints every licence text in full.

entries.headline: Scheduled jobs are declared in nvs.toml and run as ordinary scripts
entries.body: A schedule entry in the server's configuration names a five-field cron expression and a script, which runs in a fresh sandbox when the time comes. There is no scheduling API and nothing a program can register at run time. One key is mandatory with no default: scope, either "fleet", once across the deployment with the shared store as the lock, or "host", once on every machine. Fleet scope without a shared store refuses to boot. A missed fire is not caught up, and fleet scope means at most once, not exactly once.

entries.headline: Server config reloads over a local socket, and a request never sees it change
entries.body: The parsed configuration is one read-only snapshot; a request copies it when it starts and is unaffected by anything afterwards. `nvs ctl reload` re-reads `nvs.toml` through a local socket only — no network port, token or TLS, because the socket's owner and permissions are the authentication. The whole file is validated before anything is published, and a broken file leaves the running snapshot untouched. Every setting says whether it applies on reload or only at boot, and a reload names the boot-only settings it could not apply.

entries.headline: A package is its hash, the highest minimum wins, and nothing runs on install
entries.body: A package is identified by the hash of its contents; a name is only a way to find one. A published package may depend only on registry packages, so no git URL reaches you through a dependency. Each dependency names a minimum and the build takes the highest minimum anyone asked for: no solver, no unsolvable graph. No install script ever runs before your program does. Each package declares the permissions it wants, you grant them one line per package, and a call needing an ungranted one stops the build.

entries.headline: The API document is generated while building and cannot drift from the code
entries.body: The compiler already knows every route and already derives a serialization codec from each class's declared properties. An OpenAPI 3.1 document is those two facts written out, produced by `nvs build --openapi` and never maintained by hand, so it cannot disagree with the code. What the types cannot say — a summary, an error response, a security scheme — comes from an `#[Api]` attribute and the doc comment, and an `#[Api]` that contradicts the code stops the build. `nvs api diff` fails the build on a breaking change.

entries.headline: PHP conversion is one rule table with two modes, and every line is graded
entries.body: `nvs convert` translates PHP with one table of graded rules: proven to behave identically, mechanically translatable but possibly different, or no mechanical translation at all. The default mode emits only proven rules and comments out everything else with the idiomatic Novis replacement beside it — a worklist that will not run. The runnable mode also emits the possibly-different rules, each marked with a `TODO` naming how it may differ. A rule is "proven" only when a test against real PHP backs it, so the correctness number is measured, never asserted.

entries.headline: Two run modes, production by default, and a mode is only a list of defaults
entries.body: A server runs in `development` or `production`, nothing else, and with nothing configured it runs in production. A mode is shorthand for the defaults of eight named settings — logging, error detail, debug output, static files, code revalidation — and hides no other behaviour; every setting stays individually settable. The mode is set in the root-owned `nvs.toml` or by `nvs serve --mode=`, never by an environment variable. A program may flip the request-level settings for its own request, under a ceiling that defaults to the mode the server started in.

entries.headline: A service install stores one command line, and the installer fails closed
entries.body: Installing Novis as a service registers the binary with the platform's service manager and stores the command line after `--` verbatim, so any option the binary accepts is available to a service. Because a privileged account runs that line at every boot, the installer refuses anything doubtful: only serving and running may be hosted, no relative paths, no install whose output goes nowhere, no password on a command line. On Windows the service runs under a per-service virtual account; on Linux the tool prints a hardened systemd unit and writing it is an explicit opt-in.

entries.headline: One grammar serves editor and compiler, and an editor answer is a frozen test
entries.body: The editor's language server has no second, error-tolerant parser. The one grammar already yields a tree for any input, however broken; the editor mode adds only the comments and whitespace the compiler discards, so a file can be rebuilt byte for byte, plus an index that answers what sits under the cursor. `nvs check` and `nvs run` are that same parse followed by refusing if anything was reported. An editor answer is frozen the way program output is: a case file holds a document with a cursor marker, a request and the expected response.

entries.headline: In the editor a secret is blurred by default; a tainted value is not marked
entries.body: A literal or interpolated value whose type carries `secret` is blurred in place in the editor, so a screen share does not see it. The language server computes the ranges; the editor only draws them. Only the value is concealed, never the variable name that binds it. Revealing is explicit, per range, and does not survive closing the editor. Tainted values get no decoration by default: a tainted value on a screen is not a security event, a credential on a stream is. The bytes still stay in the file.

entries.headline: Configuration is a tree of TOML files, and file ownership decides trust
entries.body: Configuration is a tree of TOML files. A root is named on the command line or found as `nvs.toml`, and it pulls in more files with `[[include]]`, by path or by directory. Resolution is one ordered stream — each file's own keys, then its includes, depth first — and later wins, so an included file overrides the one that included it. Every file is trusted as far as its ownership: a file writable by any account but its owner refuses to boot. A secret arrives as a file whose whole content is the value.

entries.headline: An application is its entry file, and per-app settings are keyed on that path
entries.body: An application is the path of the file that starts it, so a command-line run has an identity just as a served request does. A per-application block, `[[app]]`, names either a `root` directory covering every entry file beneath it or a single `entry` file, resolved to its real location first so no `..` segment and no symlink inherits another application's rights. Every matching block applies, least specific first. A block may widen as well as narrow — raising a limit up to the global hard ceiling, or granting a capability the global settings withhold.

entries.headline: The editor completes only what the compiler already knows
entries.body: Find references, highlight occurrences, code lenses above a declaration, the type hierarchy and the dimming of unused private members are all queries against one reference index the language server builds. Completion of values the program itself defines — a route name, a configuration directive — is offered only where the compiler already derives that value for its own reasons, never from scanning a directory layout or a naming convention; that keeps framework guesswork out of the server. The HTML half of a file gets the editor's own HTML and CSS services but no second formatter.

entries.headline: Typing a PHP function name in the editor offers its Novis replacement
entries.body: Someone arriving from PHP types the name they already know, and the editor answers with the Novis one. The candidates come from the complete inventory of PHP built-ins, so every PHP name appears from the first day: a missing name would read as "Novis cannot do this", while one marked not yet classified reads as an audited gap with an answer owed. An item inserts only a library member that exists in the current build, so a promised but unbuilt destination is shown and inert.

entries.headline: The editor can narrow `array<mixed>` to the type a literal actually holds
entries.body: Writing `array<array<array<float>>>` by hand is tedious, so a nested literal often gets annotated `array<mixed>` and loses type checking for good. The editor offers a fix: on an array literal right there in the source, it works out the narrowest type covering every element and proposes the spelling you could have typed. It answers only from the literal itself, declines when the value comes from input or would still be `mixed`, and always presents a diff to approve, never a silent change on save. The compiler never uses this; the language is unchanged.

entries.headline: Telemetry is off by default, and a process serving traffic never uploads
entries.body: Two switches, both off until the operator turns them on: usage telemetry and the update check. Each `nvs` command then adds one to a local counter for the subcommand that ran, never its arguments and never anything about the requests a server handled. At most once a week the previous week's totals ride along with a short command, commonly the update check. A serving process only counts; it never uploads. An upload cannot fail the command carrying it, and `nvs telemetry show` prints what would be sent.

entries.headline: A doc comment is `///`, and its only tags are `@see` and `@example`
entries.body: A documentation comment starts with `///`; four slashes or more is an ordinary comment. Inside is Markdown prose plus exactly two tags, `@see` naming a member and `@example` naming a file, and any other `@tag` stops the build. There is deliberately no `@param`, `@return`, `@throws` or `@var`: the signature already says the first two. The reference, the website and `nvs doc` all render the one JSON `nvs meta --json` emits. Nothing requires a doc comment by default: `nvs check --strict-docs` reports a public member without one, and publishing a package turns that on.

entries.headline: Writing a doc comment is the editor’s job, not the language’s
entries.body: A doc comment is a run of `///` lines, and the per-line marker is what stops anything inside from ending it early. What it costs is typing, and both halves of that belong to the editor: pressing Enter inside a doc comment starts the next line, and pasting several lines in offers to prefix them all. Neither adds a setting or a command. The alternative — a block form writing the marker once at each end — was turned down: its closing marker is what a code example inside the comment would contain.

entries.headline: The nvs command line drops inherited PHP flags, and --help names the build
entries.body: Novis copies PHP's semantics, never its command line. The one inherited flag, nvs -i, is gone, with the derived --info spelling and the global --licenses that hung off it; nvs info is now spelled one way. The -h and -V flags stay, since they come from the argument parser and Unix convention, not PHP. And --help now opens with two lines: the project title as the README states it, then the version, commit and date of the build answering. That date is the commit's, not the build's, so rebuilds stay identical.

entries.headline: The nvs help text is written for the person reading it, and names no PHP input
entries.body: The argument parser prints a command's doc comment verbatim, so those comments are the program's output rather than notes about it — and they had been written as notes, citing internal rules and pointing at documents a user cannot open. Each citation moves into an ordinary comment a line below, where the project still finds it, and what a user sees now describes the flag. In the same pass, the commands that never read a file's extension stop advertising a .php input, and the one that does read it stops taking one.

entries.headline: The editor extension ships no compiler, and a missing one is a guided install
entries.body: The VS Code extension does not bundle `nvs`. It looks in the `nvs.path` setting, then on the `PATH`, then in a copy it manages itself, and when none is found it offers two commands rather than an error about environment variables: one downloads the release matching the extension's own version series and checks every byte against that release's published checksums, the other opens the release page so you can verify the bytes yourself. Nothing is fetched unless you run the command, and the managed copy never rewrites your settings.

entries.headline: The debug viewer is a separate service that reads files the application wrote
entries.body: An application writes debug records to a spool file it owns alone and opens no socket for them; a separate service ingests those files continuously and serves a viewer that only reads. The viewer renders the one thing no existing tool does, the live stream of correlated requests, and hands any artifact that already has a good viewer, such as a profile, to that viewer. Writing the records at all is the `[debug] store` setting, off by default, and it can only reduce what is kept.

entries.headline: A coding agent learns Novis by asking the compiler, not by reading the repo
entries.body: `nvs agent` prints a short primer, searches a one-line-per-member index of the standard library and shows a card for one member, all generated from the same registry the compiler carries. An agent reads the primer once and pays a few hundred tokens per lookup, instead of loading a reference far larger than its context. `nvs agent init` writes one pointer file per coding harness, and the pointer says where to ask and nothing about the language itself, because a stated fact is a copy that goes stale the day a member changes.

entries.headline: The language server keeps one workspace index, and hints appear in two idioms
entries.body: One index of every symbol in the workspace, keyed by the name the type checker resolved, answers workspace symbol search, references, rename, implementations and the call hierarchy. Eight more standard editor requests are supported on the same basis; go-to-declaration is refused because Novis has no declaration that is not the definition. Completion also offers names after a namespace separator and bare names in scope. Inlay hints are shown for exactly two idioms and nowhere else.

entries.headline: The editor reads the CLI's own documents; the Test Explorer is those shown
entries.body: Every machine-readable surface an editor needs is a document the command line already writes, and each is versioned once at its root. `nvs check --json` is at version 1. The test report is at version 2, where every test carries the file, line and column it is declared at, and `nvs test --list` writes the same document with no verdicts because nothing ran. The Test Explorer is built from those two: the list fills the tree, a filtered run fills in results, and the editor computes nothing the documents do not already say.

entries.headline: Format-on-save formats the HTML too, indented from the code that opened it
entries.body: Saving a `.nvs` file runs `nvs fmt` over the whole file, asks the compiler where the markup regions are, and then runs the editor's own HTML formatter over each region, starting at the indentation of the `?>` line that opened it. `nvs fmt` gains one rule to make that work: a `?>` that begins its line sits at the depth of the block it is in. Markup therefore indents from where the code is, so a file no longer jumps between the two. The pass is on by default and `nvs.template.format` turns it off.

entries.headline: The compile cache directory has one spelling; `[cache]` is the value cache
entries.body: `opcache.file_cache_dir` is where compiled programs are cached, and it is the only key that says so. `[cache] dir` used to parse and be read by nobody, so an operator who set it moved nothing and was told nothing; writing it now is an unknown-directive error naming the file and line. `[cache]` holds the settings of `Core\Cache`'s local and shared tiers and nothing else. Changing the compile cache directory takes a restart; the rest of `[opcache]` is read at the next compile.

entries.headline: A completion row reads like the declaration; a description is fetched per row
entries.body: A row in the completion list shows a method as `name(params)` with its return type at the right, a constant as `NAME = value`, and a class with its namespace in brackets after the name. The list no longer carries a description for every row: each row carries a small key, and the editor asks for the description of the one row it is showing, the same text hovering the name shows. Accepting a method writes its parentheses. Every `Core` class now carries a one-sentence card.

entries.headline: `nvs doc` names a class's parent class and interfaces
entries.body: `nvs meta --json app.nvs` now gives each class an `extends` key with its parent class and an `implements` key with its interfaces. Each name is written in full, with its namespace. `nvs doc` prints both at the top of the class page, and writes `static` in front of a static method.

entries.headline: An override uses the doc comment of the method it replaces
entries.body: `nvs check --strict-docs` no longer reports a method that implements a documented interface method or overrides a documented parent method. That method uses the parent's `///` comment. `nvs doc` shows that comment on the method and names the class or interface it comes from.

entries.headline: Test coverage reports for CI
entries.body: `nvs test --coverage-lcov <FILE>` writes which lines your tests ran, in the lcov format. `--coverage-clover <FILE>` writes the same lines as Clover XML, the format PHPUnit writes. Every line a statement starts on is listed with the number of times it ran. A line no test reached reads `0`. Coverage costs nothing in a run that does not ask for it.

entries.headline: Paths and class names complete and link in the editor
entries.body: Inside the path of a `require` or an `autoload` declaration, the editor lists the folders and `.nvs` files in the folder the path reaches, and ctrl+click on a folder shows it in the Explorer. A path you pass to a function that reads or writes a file lists every file and folder, opens the file on ctrl+click and shows its full path on hover. An `autoload` prefix lists the namespaces your code declares. A class name in a string, in `'App\User' as class<Model>` or `Core\Reflect::forClass('App\User')`, lists your classes and opens the class on ctrl+click.

entries.headline: A project can add its own completion values for any string parameter
entries.body: Put JSON files in a `.novis/completion/` folder anywhere in your project. Each file lists values and the method parameters they belong to. When you type a string at one of those parameters, the editor offers the values. Each value can have a label, an icon, a title and a Markdown description. You can write the files by hand, or generate them with any script, for example from a dataset or an icon set. The editor reloads a file when it changes. The files are only read and never run.

entries.headline: Completion values can show their source, depend on an argument and be checked
entries.body: A value in a completion file can name the file and line that define it. Hover shows its description, and ctrl+click opens that line. A list can depend on another argument, so a translation method offers only the keys of the domain you passed. Long keys such as `shop.cart.title` complete one part at a time. The editor can warn about a string not in the list. A deprecated value can name its replacement, and the editor offers to change it. A parameter typed as fixed strings, such as `'paid'|'shipped'`, completes them without a file.

entries.headline: The compiler warns where operator order is easy to misread
entries.body: `$n ?? 0 + 10` is `$n ?? (0 + 10)`, and `"n=" . $ok ? "x" : "y"` tests the whole `"n=" . $ok`. Both are valid code, so the compiler warns with `W1022` and does not stop. The warning offers two fixes: parentheses that keep what the line does now, which a save may apply, and the order the line most likely meant, which only you can choose. Nothing changes when the program runs.

entries.headline: The editor converts a string to an html literal
entries.body: Put the cursor on a string, or on a `.` chain such as `"" . $name . ""`, and choose **Convert to html literal**. The editor writes `` html`{$name}` ``, which prints the same text. The text of an html literal is printed as markup, so read the preview before you apply it. The action never runs on save.

groups.title: Engineering decisions
groups.blurb: Decisions about how Novis itself is built and measured. Real decisions, kept for the record, but a reader learning the language can skip the group entirely.

entries.headline: Performance history is an instruction count, not a stopwatch
entries.body: Two measurements exist, never mixed. Per-change guards compare one run against itself on whatever machine built it — a deep call chain against a shallow one, a throw against a return — and ask only whether a commit regressed. The history is separate: on every merge, one dedicated Linux machine runs a fixed workload under callgrind and appends the total instructions retired to a file in the repository. That number reproduces bit-for-bit across CPUs and years; a timer never does. Wall-clock time and the ratio against PHP sit beside it as context only.

entries.headline: Dependencies stay current, and a break they force is absorbed, not passed on
entries.body: Being behind on a dependency is a defect with a date on it, because the alternative is one enormous forced migration under a security deadline. Before the first numbered release, anything is updated at any time. From then on a version contract applies: a change that only breaks Novis's insides is adapted around and shipped in a patch, while one that would change something a program author can see goes through a ladder of ways to absorb it first. The update sweep is started by a person, never by an agent.

entries.headline: The runtime waits for readiness, and a task that would block parks itself
entries.body: On every platform the operating system tells the runtime when a socket is ready, and the runtime does the read or write itself. A task tries the operation first and parks only when it would block; when woken it tries again, treating the wake as a hint rather than a promise, so a warm socket pays nothing extra. A task's stack reserves a megabyte of address space but only the pages it touches cost real memory; stacks are pooled per worker and charged to the request, so memory tracks work in flight, not traffic served.

entries.headline: Five database drivers share one network stream and one connection model
entries.body: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite and SQL Server each get a driver that speaks its protocol itself over the runtime's own network stream, so no driver brings an async runtime of its own, and all share the one TLS client. Whether a connection is busy is tracked on the connection, not the stream. A connection whose wire is not at a clean message boundary is closed rather than reset, because a reset written into the middle of another message proves nothing. The drivers are a fixed set with one branch per operation, not a plug-in interface.

entries.headline: A feature is finished when it has tests, examples, a cost and a hostile case
entries.body: A shipped feature owes four things: tests in Novis and in Rust that pin its behaviour; three short examples showing what it is for; one benchmark giving it a measured cost against Novis's own history, never PHP; and one program written to break it, which passes when the runtime is still standing. The list of features is derived from the binary's own metadata, never kept by hand, so a new feature owes its proofs on the next sweep and a deleted one stops owing them. A failing proof is fixed or recorded, never weakened.

entries.headline: A connection is one future, polled by the coroutine that accepted it
entries.body: Inside the server each connection is a single future, and the coroutine that accepted it drives it in a loop: clear the flag, poll, park. A waker is not a scheduler; it is permission for one more poll, delivered to the parked task on its own core and issued again only after it fires. Nothing is spawned, nothing is queued, and a wake from another core wakes the task without moving it, so this is not a second scheduler. A cancellation ends the loop, and off a core driving a future blocks the thread.

entries.headline: A push runs the checks its diff can break; the nightly runs everything
entries.body: Continuous integration has three lanes in one workflow. Every push runs the document checks, which cost seconds. Build, test, conformance and lint run on all three platforms whenever any code changes; the memory checker, dependency licensing and the reference check run only when a diff can affect them. Every night and at every release all of it runs, plus Miri, the fuzzers and the unsafe audit. No lane is ever narrowed by platform. The trade: a bug only Miri or a fuzzer sees is found within a day, not ten minutes.

entries.headline: A rule about what the editor draws belongs to the editor chapter
entries.body: The rulebook's security chapter holds only rules that still hold with no editor running: what the compiler refuses, what a running program can reach. Rules about blurring a secret on screen, the editor's dependency allowlist or which server version a client accepts moved to the editor chapter, where they sit together as one section on security in the editor. No rule was weakened or changed; five rules changed address so that a reader of the ground rules can tell a compiler guarantee from an editor convenience.

entries.headline: On SQLite a queue claim is an immediate transaction, and that is the lock
entries.body: SQLite has a single writer, so inside an immediate transaction no other connection is writing and two workers cannot claim the same job; the row-locking clause the other databases use would do nothing there and is not written. The transaction is opened as immediate rather than deferred because a read followed by a write would otherwise try to upgrade a shared lock, which SQLite refuses without waiting. Nothing about this is visible from a program.

entries.headline: An idle server does no work
entries.body: A task can hold a wake handle for itself while it waits. When the task let such a handle go, the runtime used to queue a wake, and that wake ended the task's next wait at once. One task in the server takes a handle for every wait, so it never waited, and an idle server kept one core busy. The handle is now collected without a wake when the task it names is the one letting it go. A handle dropped by another thread still wakes its task.
